question: A company uses AWS Organizations with 40 member accounts. The security team must guarantee that no S3 bucket or object in any member account can ever be made public, even by account administrators who try to change bucket-level settings. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level in every member account.
Configure every bucket ACL as private and schedule a Lambda function to reset ACLs nightly.
Enable S3 Versioning with MFA Delete on every bucket so that policy changes require MFA.
Attach a service control policy that denies s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock to all principals in the member accounts.
Create an S3 Access Point for each bucket and remove the bucket endpoints.
explanation: Account-level Block Public Access overrides any bucket policy or ACL that would grant public access, and an SCP that denies s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock prevents administrators in member accounts from turning those settings off. Resetting ACLs on a schedule is reactive and leaves windows of exposure. MFA Delete protects object versions and the versioning state, not bucket policies or ACLs. Access points do not remove the bucket endpoint.

question: A logistics company receives shipment manifests from a partner that writes objects into the company's S3 bucket from the partner's own AWS account. The company's analytics jobs receive Access Denied errors on some of those objects because the partner account owns them. The company wants every object in the bucket to be owned by the bucket owner and wants to manage access only through policies. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Require the partner to add the bucket-owner-full-control canned ACL to every upload request.
Set S3 Object Ownership on the bucket to Bucket owner enforced.
Enable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket and ask the partner to upload the objects again.
Create an S3 Access Point for the partner with a policy that grants s3:PutObjectAcl.
explanation: The Bucket owner enforced setting disables ACLs and makes the bucket owner the owner of every object automatically, so access is controlled only with policies. Requiring a canned ACL depends on the partner's code being correct and keeps ACLs in use. Block Public Access does not change object ownership. Granting s3:PutObjectAcl keeps the ACL model the company wants to avoid.

question: A company's policy states that it must generate and manage its own encryption keys outside AWS and supply the key with each request. AWS must use the key only to encrypt or decrypt the object and must not store the key. Which S3 encryption option meets this requirement?
options: SSE-S3
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
SSE-C
DSSE-KMS
explanation: With SSE-C the client sends its own key in each request, S3 uses it to perform server-side encryption or decryption, and then discards the key, storing only a salted HMAC to validate future requests. SSE-S3 uses keys that S3 manages. SSE-KMS and DSSE-KMS use keys stored in AWS KMS, so AWS holds the key. Since April 2026, SSE-C is blocked by default on new general purpose buckets, so a bucket must first allow it by setting BlockedEncryptionTypes to NONE in its default encryption configuration.

question: A healthcare company stores patient records in an S3 bucket. Compliance rules state that the cloud operations team, which administers the bucket, must not be able to read the record contents. A separate security team must control who can use the encryption key, and every use of the key must be auditable. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use SSE-S3 and add a bucket policy that explicitly denies s3:GetObject to the operations team, with CloudTrail data events logging every object read.
Use SSE-C with keys stored in AWS Secrets Manager under a resource policy owned by the security team, and let the operations team retrieve the keys for uploads.
Use SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key aws/s3 and attach IAM policies that deny the operations team kms:Decrypt, with CloudTrail logging each key use.
Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key whose key policy the security team administers and that allows kms:Decrypt only for the application role.
explanation: A customer managed KMS key lets the security team own the key policy, so even users with full S3 permissions cannot decrypt objects without kms:Decrypt, and AWS CloudTrail records every key use. SSE-S3 offers no separate key permission, so a bucket administrator could change the bucket policy and read data. Giving the operations team access to SSE-C keys defeats the separation. The AWS managed key policy cannot be edited, so the security team cannot control who uses it.

question: A mobile photo-sharing application lets users upload images directly to a private S3 bucket. The application users do not have AWS credentials, and each upload link must stop working 10 minutes after it is issued. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Have the backend generate a presigned URL for a PutObject request with a 10-minute expiration and return it to the app.
Grant public write access on the upload prefix through the bucket policy and add a lifecycle rule that deletes objects 10 minutes after upload.
Ensure that the IAM role used by the backend to sign the URL has s3:PutObject permission on the upload prefix.
Embed long-term IAM user access keys scoped to s3:PutObject on the upload prefix in the mobile app so it can call S3 directly.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and hand out the accelerate endpoint, whose upload links expire automatically after 10 minutes.
explanation: A presigned URL carries the signer's permissions for a limited time, so the backend can issue a 10-minute PutObject URL and the bucket stays private. The signing principal must itself be allowed to perform s3:PutObject, otherwise the presigned request fails. Public write access and embedded long-term keys are insecure. Transfer Acceleration improves upload speed and has nothing to do with link expiration.

question: A video production company has editors in Australia, Brazil, and Germany who upload multi-gigabyte raw footage files over the public internet to a single S3 bucket in us-east-1. Uploads from the distant offices are slow and inconsistent. The company wants to improve upload speed without changing where the data is stored. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and have clients upload through the accelerate endpoint.
Configure Cross-Region Replication to buckets on each continent and have editors upload to the us-east-1 bucket.
Create an S3 gateway endpoint for each office network.
Change the default storage class of uploads to S3 Express One Zone.
explanation: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads to the nearest CloudFront edge location and then over the optimized AWS backbone to the bucket Region, which speeds long-distance transfers. Replication copies data after it lands and does not speed the original upload. Gateway endpoints work only for traffic from within a VPC, not from office networks. S3 Express One Zone is a directory bucket class for low-latency in-AZ access and does not help remote internet uploads.

question: A media company's application uploads 20 GB video files to Amazon S3 using a single PUT request, and the uploads fail. The company needs the uploads to succeed and to be resilient to transient network errors. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.
Use the multipart upload API to upload the file as parts in parallel.
Compress each file before upload so that it fits within a single request.
Request a service quota increase for the maximum single PUT object size.
explanation: A single PUT is limited to 5 GB, so large objects must use multipart upload, which also lets parts upload in parallel and retry individually after a failure. Transfer Acceleration does not change the single PUT size limit. Compression is not guaranteed to bring video below the limit and is not a reliable design. The single PUT size limit is not an adjustable quota.

question: A data engineering team notices that the storage bill for an ingestion bucket keeps rising even though the number of visible objects is stable. Investigation shows that many large uploads from unreliable networks fail partway through and are never completed. Which solution will reduce cost with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Change the default storage class of the bucket to S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
Enable versioning and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions.
Add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads 7 days after initiation.
Enable S3 Requester Pays so that the uploading clients pay for the storage.
explanation: Parts of incomplete multipart uploads are stored and billed but do not appear as objects, and a lifecycle AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action removes them automatically. Intelligent-Tiering does not delete unfinished upload parts. Noncurrent version expiration affects completed object versions, not upload parts. Requester Pays shifts request and transfer charges, not storage charges.

question: Developers at a marketing agency sometimes overwrite or delete campaign assets in an S3 bucket by mistake. The agency wants to be able to restore any earlier copy of an object quickly. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure Same-Region Replication to a second bucket.
Enable S3 server access logging to record every overwrite.
Apply S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 1-year retention period to every object.
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket.
explanation: Versioning keeps every version of an object, so an overwritten object can be restored and a delete only adds a delete marker that can be removed. Replication also replicates overwrites and adds a second bucket to manage. Access logs record requests but cannot restore data. Compliance mode Object Lock is far stricter than needed and prevents anyone from removing versions during the retention period.

question: Auditors require that an S3 bucket's own versioning configuration enforce multi-factor authentication before anyone can permanently delete an object version or suspend versioning. Which action will meet this requirement?
options: Use the root user credentials and MFA device to enable MFA Delete on the bucket by using the AWS CLI or API.
Sign in to the S3 console as an IAM administrator with MFA and enable MFA Delete in the bucket properties.
Attach an IAM policy with an aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition to all users and enable Object Lock in governance mode.
Add a lifecycle configuration rule that requires MFA for expiration actions.
explanation: MFA Delete is part of the versioning configuration and can be enabled only by the bucket owner's root user, using the root MFA device through the CLI or API. The S3 console cannot enable MFA Delete, and IAM users cannot enable it. IAM conditions and Object Lock can add protection but are not the versioning-level MFA requirement the auditors asked for. Lifecycle rules have no MFA setting.

question: A bank stores scanned loan documents in S3 Standard. Documents are accessed often for 30 days after upload, then about once per quarter, and every access must return data within milliseconds. The documents must survive the loss of an Availability Zone and must be deleted after 5 years. Which combination of lifecycle actions is MOST cost-effective? (Select TWO.)
options: Transition objects to S3 One Zone-IA 30 days after creation.
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval 30 days after creation.
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive 30 days after creation.
Add an expiration action that deletes objects 1,825 days after creation.
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval 30 days after creation.
explanation: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval offers millisecond access and multi-AZ resilience at a lower storage price than Standard-IA for data accessed about once a quarter, and an expiration action removes objects after 5 years. One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ and would not survive an AZ loss. Glacier Deep Archive and Glacier Flexible Retrieval require a restore that takes minutes to hours, so they do not meet the millisecond requirement.

question: A startup stores user-generated content whose access patterns are unpredictable: some objects are popular for months and others are never read again. The startup wants to minimize storage cost automatically without paying retrieval fees when data is accessed. Which storage class should it use?
options: S3 Standard-IA
S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers based on observed access and charges a small monitoring fee but no retrieval fees. Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, and Glacier Instant Retrieval all charge per-GB retrieval fees, which can be expensive for objects that turn out to be popular. One Zone-IA also reduces resilience.

question: An insurance company must retain closed claim files for 10 years to satisfy regulators. The files are almost never read, and when an auditor requests one, a retrieval time of up to 48 hours is acceptable. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective?
options: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive has the lowest storage price in S3 and supports standard retrievals within 12 hours and bulk retrievals within 48 hours, which fits the requirement. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Instant Retrieval cost more to store and offer faster access that is not needed. Standard-IA is designed for data that needs millisecond access and is considerably more expensive for long-term archives.

question: An e-commerce company generates product image thumbnails from originals that are stored safely in another bucket. The thumbnails are accessed infrequently, must load in milliseconds when requested, and can be regenerated if lost. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective for the thumbnails?
options: S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
explanation: One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA and still provides millisecond access, and the single-AZ risk is acceptable because the thumbnails can be recreated. Standard-IA pays for multi-AZ resilience that is not needed. Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires a restore before access. Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring charge and keeps data in multi-AZ tiers, which is unnecessary for re-creatable infrequent data.

question: A machine learning team runs training jobs on a large fleet of EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. The jobs read millions of small files and need consistent single-digit millisecond latency at hundreds of thousands of requests per second. Which storage option will provide the HIGHEST performance?
options: An S3 Standard bucket with Transfer Acceleration enabled so requests are routed through the nearest edge location
An S3 Express One Zone directory bucket in the same Availability Zone as the instances
An S3 One Zone-IA bucket in the same Region, which stores the data in a single Availability Zone
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage, which returns objects with millisecond access like S3 Standard
explanation: S3 Express One Zone uses directory buckets in a chosen Availability Zone and is designed for consistent single-digit millisecond latency and very high request rates, which suits co-located training jobs. Transfer Acceleration improves long-distance internet transfers, not in-Region latency. One Zone-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval are lower-cost classes for infrequent access and do not provide this level of performance.

question: A company must encrypt objects in a data lake bucket with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Applications write and read millions of small objects per day, and the AWS KMS portion of the bill has become larger than the S3 storage cost. Which solution will reduce cost while keeping the customer managed key?
options: Switch the bucket to SSE-C and have each application supply its own encryption key with every request.
Replace the key with a customer managed multi-Region KMS key that has a replica key in a second Region.
Enable S3 Bucket Keys in the bucket's SSE-KMS default encryption configuration.
Create a separate KMS grant for each application role instead of listing the roles in the key policy.
explanation: An S3 Bucket Key is a bucket-level key generated from the KMS key that S3 uses to create data keys, which cuts the number of KMS requests and their cost significantly while still using the customer managed key. SSE-C would drop the KMS requirement and add key management burden. Multi-Region keys and grants do not reduce the number of KMS calls.

question: A financial services company must keep a copy of trade confirmation files in a second AWS Region for disaster recovery. Regulators require that the company demonstrate that 99.99% of new objects are copied within 15 minutes and that replication delays generate alerts. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure Same-Region Replication with versioning enabled.
Run S3 Batch Operations copy jobs every 15 minutes.
Configure Cross-Region Replication and enable Transfer Acceleration on both buckets.
Configure Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control enabled.
explanation: S3 Replication Time Control is backed by an SLA to replicate 99.99% of objects within 15 minutes and provides replication metrics and event notifications for objects that miss the threshold. Same-Region Replication does not put a copy in another Region. Scheduled Batch Operations jobs add overhead and provide no SLA. Transfer Acceleration does not affect replication timing.

question: A company enabled Cross-Region Replication on a bucket that already contained 300 million objects. New objects are replicating, but the existing objects are not present in the destination bucket. Which solution will copy the existing objects with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use S3 Batch Replication to replicate the existing objects.
Suspend and then re-enable versioning on the source bucket.
Enable S3 Replication Time Control on the replication rule.
Add a lifecycle rule that transitions existing objects to a new storage class to trigger replication.
explanation: Live replication applies only to objects written after the rule is created, and S3 Batch Replication is the managed way to replicate existing objects, as well as objects that previously failed to replicate. Toggling versioning does not replicate anything. RTC affects only new objects. Lifecycle transitions are not replicated and do not trigger replication of the object.

question: A company configured Cross-Region Replication from a bucket in eu-west-1 to a bucket in eu-central-1. Objects encrypted with SSE-S3 replicate successfully, but objects encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key are not replicated. Which combination of actions will resolve the issue? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on both buckets so that replicated objects travel over the AWS edge network.
In the replication rule, opt in to replicating objects encrypted with AWS KMS and specify a KMS key in eu-central-1 for the replicas.
Enable S3 Object Lock on the destination bucket so that the replicas keep the same retention settings as the source objects.
Grant the replication IAM role kms:Decrypt on the source key and kms:Encrypt on the destination key.
Disable S3 Bucket Keys on the destination bucket so that each replica gets its own data key from the destination KMS key.
explanation: S3 replicates SSE-KMS objects only when the rule explicitly opts in to KMS-encrypted objects and names a destination KMS key, and the replication role must be able to decrypt with the source key and encrypt with the destination key. Transfer Acceleration does not affect replication. Object Lock adds retention, not KMS permissions. Bucket Keys are compatible with replication and disabling them does not fix missing permissions.

question: A payments company encrypts records on the client side in us-east-1 before storing them in S3, and the records are replicated to eu-west-1. Applications in eu-west-1 must be able to decrypt the records using a key in their own Region, without calling AWS KMS in us-east-1 and without re-encrypting the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a single-Region KMS key in each Region and copy the AWS-generated key material from the us-east-1 key into the eu-west-1 key.
Create a multi-Region primary key in us-east-1 and a replica key in eu-west-1, and use them for encryption and decryption.
Use the AWS managed key aws/s3 in both Regions, which AWS creates automatically in each Region the first time S3 uses it.
Grant the eu-west-1 application roles kms:Decrypt on the us-east-1 key and call it through the us-east-1 KMS endpoint.
explanation: Multi-Region keys share the same key ID and key material across Regions, so data encrypted with the primary key can be decrypted locally with the replica key. AWS-generated key material cannot be exported to another key, and separate single-Region keys are not interchangeable. AWS managed keys are different in each Region and cannot be used for client-side encryption. Cross-Region calls violate the requirement to avoid a dependency on us-east-1.

question: Which statement correctly describes envelope encryption as used by AWS KMS and Amazon S3 server-side encryption?
options: AWS KMS encrypts the entire object payload directly with the KMS key, and S3 stores the ciphertext together with the key ID.
The object is encrypted twice, first with an S3-managed key and then with a KMS key in a second Region for added redundancy.
The object is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is encrypted with a KMS key and stored alongside the encrypted object.
The KMS key material is exported to the client over TLS, which uses it to encrypt the object locally and then discards it.
explanation: In envelope encryption, a data key encrypts the data, and the KMS key encrypts only the data key, which is stored with the ciphertext so it can later be decrypted by KMS. The KMS Encrypt API can directly encrypt only small payloads of up to 4 KB, so it is not used for whole objects. Double encryption across Regions is not envelope encryption. KMS key material never leaves AWS KMS unencrypted.

question: A nightly batch job runs under a temporary IAM role and must decrypt SSE-KMS objects for the duration of the job only. The security team does not want to edit the KMS key policy before and after every run. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Edit the key policy before each job to add the role with kms:Decrypt, and remove that statement after the job ends.
Schedule the KMS key for deletion after each job with the minimum 7-day waiting period and create a new key for the next run.
Disable automatic key rotation while the job runs so that the role keeps decrypting with the same key material.
Create a KMS grant that allows the role to use kms:Decrypt and retire the grant when the job finishes.
explanation: Grants provide programmatic, temporary delegation of specific KMS operations to a principal and can be retired or revoked when no longer needed, without changing the key policy. Editing the key policy every run is exactly what the team wants to avoid and is error prone. Deleting keys would make existing data unreadable. Rotation settings do not control who can use the key.

question: Account A owns an S3 bucket whose objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key in Account A. An application role in Account B must read the objects. Which combination of steps is required? (Select THREE.)
options: Add a bucket policy in Account A that grants the Account B role s3:GetObject on the bucket objects.
Re-encrypt the objects with the AWS managed key aws/s3 so that Account B can decrypt them through its S3 permissions alone.
Add a statement to the KMS key policy in Account A that allows the Account B role to use kms:Decrypt.
Enable S3 Requester Pays on the bucket so that Account B pays for the GET requests and data transfer it generates.
Attach an IAM policy to the role in Account B that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket and kms:Decrypt on the key ARN.
Create a KMS grant from Account B that names the role and the key ARN, without changing any policy in Account A.
explanation: Cross-account access needs permission on both sides for both services: the bucket policy and key policy in Account A must trust the Account B role, and the role's IAM policy in Account B must allow the S3 and KMS actions. AWS managed keys cannot be shared across accounts because their key policies cannot be modified. Requester Pays only changes who is billed. Account B cannot create a grant on the key unless Account A's key policy first allows it.

question: A defense contractor's compliance framework requires that data at rest in Amazon S3 be protected by two independent layers of server-side encryption. The company wants AWS to manage the encryption process. Which option meets this requirement?
options: Dual-layer server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (DSSE-KMS)
SSE-KMS with S3 Bucket Keys, where a bucket-level key encrypts each object's data key
SSE-S3 with S3 Versioning enabled so that every object version is encrypted
SSE-C with customer-provided AES-256 keys that are rotated on a schedule
explanation: DSSE-KMS applies two independent layers of AES-256 encryption on the server side using AWS KMS keys, designed for frameworks that require multilayer encryption. SSE-KMS with Bucket Keys is a single layer that reduces KMS calls. Versioning is unrelated to encryption layers. SSE-C is a single layer, and key rotation is the customer's responsibility.

question: A law firm will archive case files in Amazon S3. Its policy states that data must already be encrypted before it leaves the firm's on-premises network and that AWS must never have access to the plaintext. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key whose key policy grants kms:Decrypt only to the firm's on-premises role.
Encrypt the files on premises with the Amazon S3 Encryption Client and firm-controlled keys before uploading them.
Enforce SSE-S3 with a bucket policy that rejects any upload missing the x-amz-server-side-encryption header.
Add a bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SecureTransport is false so that uploads are encrypted with TLS.
explanation: Client-side encryption encrypts the data before upload, so S3 only ever receives ciphertext. SSE-KMS and SSE-S3 are server-side, meaning S3 receives the plaintext over TLS and encrypts it in AWS. Requiring TLS protects data in transit but does not keep plaintext away from AWS.

question: A security audit found that some legacy clients access an S3 bucket over plain HTTP. The company must reject any request to the bucket that is not sent over TLS. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS on the bucket so that every new object is encrypted with a customer managed key.
Enable all four S3 Block Public Access settings on the bucket to reject requests from unauthenticated legacy clients.
Add a bucket policy statement that denies all S3 actions when the aws:SecureTransport condition key is false.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and require the legacy clients to switch to the s3-accelerate endpoint for all requests.
explanation: A bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false blocks any non-TLS request regardless of other permissions. Default encryption protects data at rest, not in transit. Block Public Access controls public grants, not the protocol. Transfer Acceleration is an optional endpoint and does not stop clients from using the standard HTTP endpoint.

question: A company requires that every object uploaded to a bucket be encrypted with one approved customer managed KMS key. Several teams upload by using their own scripts, and some scripts specify a different KMS key in the request headers. Which solution enforces the requirement?
options: Configure default bucket encryption with the approved key and enable S3 Bucket Keys so that every upload is encrypted with that key.
Enable S3 Bucket Keys on the bucket so that all objects share one bucket-level key generated from the approved KMS key.
Enable automatic rotation on the approved customer managed key and allow only the uploading roles to use it in its key policy.
Add a bucket policy that denies s3:PutObject when s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id is not the approved key ARN, so uploads must name that key.
explanation: A deny statement on the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id condition key rejects any upload that names a different key, so only the approved key can be used. Default encryption applies only when a request does not specify encryption headers, so requests that name another key would still succeed. Bucket Keys reduce KMS calls and rotation changes key material, and neither restricts which key is used.

question: A company serves a single-page web application from an S3 bucket through Amazon CloudFront. The bucket must remain private with S3 Block Public Access turned on, and users must not be able to bypass CloudFront to read objects directly from S3. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Configure an origin access control (OAC) on the CloudFront distribution for the S3 REST API origin.
Enable static website hosting and use the website endpoint as the CloudFront origin.
Grant public read access through object ACLs and restrict access with a CloudFront geographic restriction.
Add a bucket policy that allows the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal to call s3:GetObject when AWS:SourceArn matches the distribution ARN.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and give the accelerate endpoint to CloudFront.
explanation: OAC lets CloudFront sign requests to the private S3 origin, and the bucket policy that allows only the CloudFront service principal for that specific distribution ensures that direct S3 requests are denied. The S3 website endpoint does not support OAC and requires public read access. Public ACLs violate the private bucket requirement and allow direct access. Transfer Acceleration is for faster uploads and does not control access.

question: A nonprofit hosts its public website on an S3 static website endpoint. The organization must now serve the site over HTTPS on its custom domain www.example.org, which is managed in Amazon Route 53. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Request a public ACM certificate for www.example.org, associate it with the S3 bucket, and enable HTTPS on the website endpoint.
Put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket with an ACM certificate from us-east-1, and create a Route 53 alias record for the distribution.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and point a Route 53 CNAME record at the HTTPS s3-accelerate endpoint for the website.
Create a Route 53 alias record that points directly to the S3 website endpoint and enable HTTPS on the record with an ACM certificate.
explanation: S3 website endpoints support only HTTP, so HTTPS with a custom domain is provided by CloudFront using an ACM certificate, which for CloudFront must be in us-east-1. Certificates cannot be attached to S3 buckets. Transfer Acceleration is not a website hosting endpoint. Route 53 records have no HTTPS setting; they only resolve names.

question: A ticketing company runs its web application behind an Application Load Balancer. If the application becomes unhealthy, the company wants users to automatically see a static maintenance page instead of an error, with minimal infrastructure to maintain. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the ALB UnHealthyHostCount metric that launches a standby EC2 instance in another Region to serve the page.
Use Route 53 weighted routing with a health check on the ALB to split traffic evenly between the ALB and an S3 static website hosting the page.
Use Route 53 failover routing: a health-checked primary record for the ALB and a secondary alias record for an S3 static website with the page.
Enable Cross-Region Replication on the website bucket and use Route 53 latency-based routing between the ALB and the replica bucket.
explanation: Failover routing sends traffic to the secondary S3 website only when the health check marks the primary ALB unhealthy, and S3 static hosting needs no servers. Launching EC2 instances adds infrastructure and delay. Weighted routing sends half of the users to the maintenance page even when the application is healthy. Replication and latency routing do not detect application failures.

question: A web application served from https://app.example.com uses browser JavaScript to fetch JSON configuration files from an S3 bucket at its S3 endpoint. Requests from the browser fail with errors stating that the origin is not allowed, although the same requests succeed from a command-line tool. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Make the bucket public with a bucket policy that grants s3:GetObject to everyone so the browser no longer needs credentials.
Enable static website hosting on the bucket and have the app load the files from the website endpoint instead.
Generate presigned URLs for each configuration file so that the browser requests carry their own authorization.
Add a CORS configuration to the bucket that allows GET requests from the https://app.example.com origin.
explanation: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy for cross-origin script requests, and S3 returns the required Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers only when the bucket has a matching CORS rule. Making the bucket public does not add CORS headers and weakens security. Static website hosting and presigned URLs do not by themselves satisfy a browser's cross-origin check.

question: A research institute shares one large S3 bucket with 25 teams, each of which needs different permissions on different prefixes. The bucket policy has become difficult to manage and is approaching its size limit. Which solution will simplify access management with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an S3 access point per team with its own access point policy, and delegate access control from the bucket policy to the access points.
Create a separate bucket for each team with its own bucket policy, and keep the data in sync with S3 Same-Region Replication.
Re-enable ACLs on the bucket and use object ACLs to grant each team's canonical user ID access to the objects under its prefix.
Create an IAM group for each team and attach a copy of the bucket policy, including its Principal elements, to each group.
explanation: Access points give each team a dedicated endpoint and policy, so permissions are managed per team instead of in one large bucket policy. Separate replicated buckets duplicate data and add cost and complexity. ACLs are disabled by default and are not granular per prefix. Bucket policies are resource policies and cannot be attached to IAM groups.

question: An analytics team must access a shared dataset bucket only from inside its VPC. Other teams access the same bucket from other networks, and their access must not be affected. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:* for every request whose aws:SourceVpc condition key does not match the analytics VPC ID.
Create an S3 access point whose network origin is the analytics VPC, and allow the analytics team access only through that access point.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 in the analytics VPC and turn on S3 Block Public Access for the bucket.
Enable S3 Object Lambda on the bucket and route the analytics team's requests through an Object Lambda Access Point.
explanation: An access point with a VPC network origin accepts requests only from the specified VPC, and its policy can scope the analytics team's permissions without changing other teams' access. A bucket-wide deny would block every other team. An interface endpoint plus Block Public Access does not restrict the analytics team to the VPC. Object Lambda transforms data and does not control network origin.

question: A retailer stores customer order records in S3. An internal analytics application needs to read the records with credit card numbers and email addresses masked, while the billing application must continue reading the original records. The retailer does not want to store and keep in sync a second copy of the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke a Lambda function that writes a masked copy of each new record to a second bucket that the analytics application reads.
Run Amazon Macie on the bucket with custom data identifiers for card numbers and email addresses so that the sensitive fields are removed from the records.
Have the analytics application call a Lambda function (through a function URL or API Gateway) that gets the original object from S3 and masks the fields before returning it.
Enable SSE-KMS with a customer managed key and use the key policy to deny the analytics application kms:Decrypt on the sensitive fields.
explanation: Invoking a Lambda function directly (through a function URL or API Gateway) lets the analytics application receive masked data on read while the billing application keeps reading the originals, and no second copy is stored. This is the alternative AWS recommends now that S3 Object Lambda is no longer available to new customers (since November 7, 2025). Writing masked copies creates the duplicate data the retailer wants to avoid. Macie discovers sensitive data but does not transform it, and KMS permissions apply to whole objects, not individual fields.

question: A global SaaS company stores customer uploads in S3 buckets in three Regions. Applications in every Region must use a single global endpoint for reads and writes that routes to the nearest bucket, and the company must be able to shift all traffic away from a Region during an outage. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create Route 53 latency-based records that point a custom domain to each Regional bucket endpoint, with health checks for failover.
Create a CloudFront distribution with an origin group containing the three buckets and rely on origin failover during an outage.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on each bucket and use the accelerate endpoints, which route requests through the nearest edge location.
Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point over the three buckets with two-way replication, and use its failover controls during an outage.
explanation: A Multi-Region Access Point gives one global endpoint that routes requests to the closest bucket over the AWS network, and failover controls let the company mark Regions active or passive in minutes; replication keeps the buckets synchronized. S3 requires requests to match bucket names, so a custom domain with latency records does not work for multiple bucket endpoints. CloudFront origin groups fail over only for reads. Transfer Acceleration endpoints are per bucket and do not provide routing or failover.

question: A compliance officer needs a daily report listing every object in a bucket of 400 million objects along with its encryption status, storage class, and replication status. The solution must not add load to the bucket through API listing calls. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure a daily S3 Inventory report that includes the encryption status, storage class, and replication status fields.
Schedule a Lambda function that calls ListObjectsV2 and HeadObject for every object each day and writes the results to a CSV file.
Enable server access logging on the bucket and query the delivered logs daily with Amazon Athena to build the report.
Use S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics and its daily metrics export, which includes encryption status and storage class data.
explanation: S3 Inventory produces scheduled flat-file lists of objects with optional metadata such as encryption status, storage class, and replication status without the caller making list requests. Listing and heading 400 million objects daily is slow and costly. Access logs show requests, not the state of every object. Storage Lens provides aggregated metrics rather than per-object listings.

question: A real estate website stores listing photos uploaded by agents in the uploads/ prefix of an S3 bucket. A thumbnail must be generated within seconds of each upload. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an EventBridge scheduled rule that runs a Lambda function every minute to list the uploads/ prefix and process new photos.
Add an S3 Event Notification for s3:ObjectCreated:* events on the uploads/ prefix that invokes a Lambda function to create the thumbnail.
Enable server access logging on the bucket and have a Lambda function parse the log files for new PUT requests under uploads/.
Replicate the uploads/ prefix to a processing bucket that an EC2 Auto Scaling group polls for new objects to resize.
explanation: S3 Event Notifications can invoke Lambda directly when objects are created under a prefix, giving near-real-time, serverless processing. A scheduled scan adds delay and repeated listing cost. Server access logs are delivered on a best-effort basis, often hours later. Replication plus EC2 polling adds infrastructure and latency.

question: Three independent microservices must each process every new object written to the invoices/ prefix of a bucket. A developer tried to create three S3 event notification configurations with the same event type and prefix, each targeting a different SQS queue, but S3 rejected the configuration. Which solution will meet the requirement in a decoupled way?
options: Create the three notification configurations with slightly different suffix filters so they do not overlap.
Replicate the bucket to three buckets and configure a separate notification on each copy.
Configure one S3 event notification to publish to an SNS topic, and subscribe the three SQS queues to the topic.
Have the first microservice forward each event to the other two microservices over HTTP.
explanation: S3 does not allow overlapping prefix and event type filters across notification configurations, so fan-out is done by publishing to an SNS topic with an SQS subscription for each consumer (or by using EventBridge rules). Changing suffix filters would cause some objects to be missed. Replicating to three buckets triples storage cost. Forwarding over HTTP couples the services and creates a single point of failure.

question: A company is deciding whether to enable Amazon EventBridge integration for an S3 bucket instead of using direct S3 event notifications. Which capabilities does EventBridge add? (Select TWO.)
options: Guaranteed exactly-once, strictly ordered delivery of every event.
Routing the same event to many targets through multiple rules.
Automatic encryption of objects at rest when events are delivered.
Removal of the need for any resource or IAM permissions on targets.
Advanced filtering on event fields such as object size or key patterns, plus event archive and replay.
explanation: With EventBridge, S3 events can be matched by many rules that each send to multiple targets, and rules support richer content filtering as well as archiving and replaying events. EventBridge does not guarantee exactly-once ordered delivery, so consumers should be idempotent. Event delivery has nothing to do with object encryption. Targets still require appropriate permissions.

question: A security team wants a low-cost record of every request made to a sensitive S3 bucket, including the requester, request time, operation, and response status, for periodic review. Which feature should the team enable?
options: S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics with activity metrics enabled
S3 Inventory reports delivered daily to a separate bucket
S3 Versioning with CloudWatch request metrics enabled
S3 server access logging to a separate logging bucket
explanation: Server access logs record detailed information about each request, such as requester, operation, key, and status, and are delivered to a target bucket at no additional charge other than storage. Storage Lens gives aggregated usage and activity metrics, not per-request records. Inventory lists objects, not requests. Versioning preserves object versions but does not log access.

question: A company changed the Object Ownership setting of its log target bucket to Bucket owner enforced so that ACLs are disabled. Afterward, S3 server access logs stopped arriving. The company requires that ACLs remain disabled. What should a solutions architect do to restore log delivery?
options: Add a target bucket policy that allows the logging.s3.amazonaws.com principal s3:PutObject, scoped to the source bucket and account.
Switch Object Ownership on the target bucket to Bucket owner preferred to re-enable ACLs, and grant the Log Delivery group write access.
Configure the source bucket to deliver its access logs to a logs/ prefix in the source bucket itself instead of the target bucket.
Switch the target bucket to SSE-C encryption so that the logging service can deliver encrypted log objects without an ACL grant.
explanation: When ACLs are disabled, log delivery permissions must be granted through a bucket policy for the logging.s3.amazonaws.com service principal, ideally with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount conditions. Re-enabling ACLs would work but violates the requirement. Logging a bucket to itself creates additional log records for every log write. SSE-C is supplied per request by a client and does not grant the logging service permission to write.

question: A brokerage firm must store trade records in a write-once-read-many (WORM) format for 7 years. No user, including the root user of the account, may delete or overwrite a record during that period. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable S3 Object Lock on the bucket, which also requires S3 Versioning.
Configure a default retention period of 7 years in governance mode.
Configure a default retention period of 7 years in compliance mode.
Enable MFA Delete and store the root MFA device in a safe.
Add a lifecycle rule that expires objects after 7 years.
explanation: S3 Object Lock provides WORM protection on versioned buckets, and compliance mode prevents any user, including the root user, from deleting or shortening retention on a locked object version until the period ends. Governance mode can be bypassed by principals with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention. MFA Delete still allows deletion by someone who has the MFA device. A lifecycle expiration rule removes data but does not prevent earlier deletion.

question: A company wants to protect backup files in S3 from deletion for 90 days. However, a small security administration team must be able to remove a backup early in exceptional cases, such as when sensitive data is uploaded by mistake. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Object Lock compliance mode with a 90-day retention period and grant only the security team role the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission.
Place an Object Lock legal hold on every backup and grant only the security team role s3:PutObjectLegalHold and s3:DeleteObject.
Use Object Lock governance mode with a 90-day retention period and grant only the security team role s3:BypassGovernanceRetention.
Enable MFA Delete on the bucket and share the root user's MFA device with the security team for early deletions.
explanation: Governance mode protects object versions from most users while allowing principals with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission to override retention when they explicitly request it. Compliance mode cannot be bypassed by anyone. Legal holds have no expiry and still need s3:PutObjectLegalHold to remove, so they do not match a 90-day requirement. Sharing root MFA is poor security practice.

question: A pharmaceutical company is involved in a lawsuit. Its legal team must ensure that specific research documents in a versioned S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled cannot be deleted until the case is closed, but no one knows how long the case will last. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Apply a compliance mode retention period of 10 years to the document versions so that they outlast any likely case.
Move the documents to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and apply an S3 Glacier Vault Lock policy that denies deletion.
Apply a governance mode retention period of 30 days and extend it every month until the case is closed.
Place an Object Lock legal hold on the document versions and remove it when the case is closed.
explanation: A legal hold protects an object version from deletion with no expiration date and stays in place until a user with s3:PutObjectLegalHold removes it, which suits indefinite litigation holds. A fixed 10-year compliance retention could not be shortened after the case ends. Vault Lock applies to S3 Glacier vaults, and changing an object's storage class does not prevent its deletion. Manually extending governance retention adds overhead and risks lapses.

question: A genomics research institute publishes a 2 PB reference dataset in S3 for other organizations that have their own AWS accounts. The institute wants the organizations that download the data to pay for the requests and data transfer. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Enable Requester Pays on the bucket.
Generate presigned URLs for each organization.
Replicate the dataset to a bucket in each organization's account.
Serve the dataset through CloudFront with signed cookies.
explanation: With Requester Pays, the requester's AWS account is charged for requests and data transfer, while the bucket owner still pays for storage. Presigned URLs bill the bucket owner for downloads. Replicating 2 PB to each account is expensive and complex. CloudFront transfer is billed to the distribution owner.

question: A data provider enabled Requester Pays on a bucket and granted a partner account read access in the bucket policy. The partner's download requests now fail with 403 Access Denied errors. What must the partner do?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration in the partner account so that the downloads are billed to the partner instead.
Include the x-amz-request-payer: requester header (or the SDK or CLI equivalent) in signed requests to accept the charges.
Send unsigned anonymous requests so that the data transfer charges are billed back to the bucket owner instead.
Ask the data provider to add the partner's canonical user ID to the bucket ACL with the payer permission.
explanation: For Requester Pays buckets, requesters must send authenticated requests that include the x-amz-request-payer header or the equivalent SDK or CLI parameter to confirm they will pay, otherwise S3 returns 403. Anonymous requests are not allowed on Requester Pays buckets. Transfer Acceleration is unrelated. There is no ACL setting that designates a payer.

question: A marketing team stores clickstream data as compressed CSV files in S3. Analysts occasionally need to run ad hoc SQL queries that return a few columns from billions of rows. The team wants the MOST cost-effective solution with no infrastructure to manage. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Load the data nightly into an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance and run the analysts' SQL queries there.
Copy the files to an EC2 Spot Instance for each query and process them with custom Python scripts.
Define a table over the S3 prefix in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and query it with Amazon Athena.
Use S3 Inventory reports in Apache Parquet format to query the contents of the CSV objects.
explanation: Athena is serverless and queries data in place in S3 using standard SQL, charging per amount of data scanned, which suits occasional ad hoc analysis. An RDS instance and EC2 scripts require provisioning and running infrastructure. S3 Inventory lists object metadata and cannot query the contents of objects.

question: Analysts query 30 TB of JSON log files in S3 with Amazon Athena, and most queries filter on a single day and read only five of 80 fields. Queries are slow and expensive. Which combination of changes will MOST improve query performance and reduce cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Move the log files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which keeps millisecond access at a lower storage price.
Convert the data to a compressed columnar format such as Apache Parquet.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket so that Athena reads the data over the edge network.
Split the data into many small files of about 1 KB each so that Athena can read them in parallel.
Partition the data in S3 by date and register the partitions in the table definition.
explanation: Columnar formats let Athena read only the needed columns and compress well, and date partitions let Athena skip data outside the queried day, so both reduce the amount of data scanned and query time. Glacier Instant Retrieval adds retrieval charges and does not reduce scanned data. Transfer Acceleration affects transfers over the internet, not Athena reads. Very small files increase overhead and slow queries.

question: A company with 120 AWS accounts wants a single view of S3 storage usage and activity across the organization, including which buckets hold large amounts of noncurrent versions or incomplete multipart uploads, so it can find cost savings. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?
options: Create an S3 Storage Lens dashboard at the organization level.
Configure S3 Inventory on every bucket and analyze the reports separately.
Review AWS Trusted Advisor checks in each account.
Enable server access logs on every bucket and query them with Athena.
explanation: S3 Storage Lens aggregates storage and activity metrics across all accounts in an organization and highlights cost optimization opportunities such as noncurrent version bytes and incomplete multipart upload bytes. Per-bucket Inventory reports require significant setup and custom analysis. Trusted Advisor has only limited S3 checks. Access logs describe requests, not storage composition.

question: An IoT platform writes sensor readings to a bucket using keys that all begin with the same prefix, for example data/reading-0001.json. At peak, writes exceed 3,500 requests per second and the application receives HTTP 503 Slow Down responses. Which change will MOST improve write throughput?
options: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that each write creates a new version instead of overwriting a key.
Spread objects across multiple prefixes, for example by adding a device ID or hash segment to the key path.
Change the storage class of new objects to S3 Standard-IA by setting the x-amz-storage-class header on each PUT.
Enable Requester Pays on the bucket so that each device is billed for its own PUT requests.
explanation: S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per partitioned prefix, so distributing keys across many prefixes lets throughput scale horizontally. Versioning does not increase request rates. Storage class does not change request throughput. Requester Pays only changes billing.

question: A geospatial application stores 50 GB raster files in S3. A processing step needs only a small header at the start of each file to decide whether to process it, and when a file is processed it must be downloaded as quickly as possible. Which approach will meet these requirements?
options: Use S3 Select with a SQL expression that returns only the header bytes of each raster file, and then call GetObject on the files to process.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket and download each file through the accelerate endpoint to inspect its header.
Use GET requests with a Range header to fetch only the header, and parallel byte-range GETs to download files that must be processed.
Use the multipart upload API with 100 MB parts to download each file in parallel parts, and read the first part as the header.
explanation: Byte-range fetches retrieve only the requested bytes, so the header can be read cheaply, and many concurrent range requests improve aggregate download throughput. S3 Select works only on CSV, JSON, and Parquet content and is not intended for binary raster files. Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance internet transfers but does not avoid downloading the full file. Multipart upload is an upload API.

question: A streaming education company stores 2 GB lecture videos in an S3 bucket in us-west-2. Students around the world report slow downloads. Which combination of actions will improve download performance? (Select TWO.)
options: Change the storage class of the videos to S3 One Zone-IA, which serves objects from a single Availability Zone.
Configure daily S3 Inventory reports for the bucket to identify the largest videos to optimize.
Serve the videos through an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as the origin.
Have the client application download each video by using parallel byte-range GET requests.
Enable MFA Delete on the bucket to protect the lecture videos.
explanation: CloudFront caches the videos at edge locations close to students, and parallel byte-range requests increase throughput for large objects. One Zone-IA is a cheaper, less resilient class and does not improve download speed. Inventory reports and MFA Delete are management and protection features with no effect on performance.

question: Which S3 storage class stores data in a single Availability Zone, so the data would be lost if that Availability Zone were destroyed?
options: S3 Standard
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 One Zone-IA
explanation: S3 One Zone-IA stores data redundantly within one Availability Zone only, so it is not resilient to the physical loss of that AZ. S3 Standard, Standard-IA, and Glacier Instant Retrieval store data across a minimum of three Availability Zones in a Region.

question: An order-processing service writes an order file to S3 and immediately lists the prefix so that a downstream step can pick up the new file. A developer added a 30-second sleep and a DynamoDB index of keys because of concerns about stale reads. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Remove the sleep and the extra index, because S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT, DELETE, and LIST.
Keep the 30-second sleep, because S3 is only eventually consistent for new objects written to a busy prefix.
Enable versioning on the bucket, because only versioned buckets provide strong consistency for LIST requests.
Keep the DynamoDB index, because S3 LIST operations are eventually consistent even though GET requests are strongly consistent.
explanation: Amazon S3 delivers strong read-after-write consistency for all GET, PUT, LIST, and DELETE operations, so a successful write is immediately visible in reads and listings. The sleep and the extra index add latency and cost without benefit. Versioning is unrelated to consistency, and LIST is no longer eventually consistent.

question: A design agency enabled versioning on a bucket of large project files. Storage costs have doubled because of old object versions. The agency must keep previous versions for 90 days for recovery, and those versions are rarely accessed but must be available within milliseconds. Which combination of lifecycle actions will reduce cost while meeting these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Transition noncurrent versions to S3 Standard-IA 30 days after they become noncurrent.
Suspend versioning on the bucket so that S3 automatically deletes the existing noncurrent versions.
Enable MFA Delete on the bucket so that noncurrent versions are removed automatically after 90 days.
Permanently delete noncurrent versions 90 days after they become noncurrent.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so that new versions upload faster and take less storage space.
explanation: Lifecycle rules can act on noncurrent versions specifically: moving them to Standard-IA after 30 days lowers storage cost while keeping millisecond access, and a NoncurrentVersionExpiration action removes them after the 90-day recovery window. Suspending versioning does not delete existing versions. MFA Delete adds protection and does not remove anything. Transfer Acceleration has no effect on storage size.

question: A bucket holds 2 billion objects. About 90% are JSON metadata files smaller than 10 KB, and the rest are images larger than 1 MB. After 30 days, objects are rarely read but must remain available within milliseconds and stored across multiple Availability Zones. Which lifecycle design is MOST cost-effective?
options: Use a lifecycle rule with an object size filter that also includes objects smaller than 128 KB so that every object transitions to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days.
Use a lifecycle rule with an object size filter so that only objects larger than 128 KB transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days.
Transition all objects to S3 One Zone-IA after 30 days.
Transition all objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
explanation: Standard-IA bills a minimum object size of 128 KB and each lifecycle transition is a charged request, so moving billions of tiny objects can cost more than leaving them in Standard; transitioning only objects larger than 128 KB moves just the large images (since September 2024 this is also the default lifecycle behavior for objects under 128 KB). Explicitly including the small files incurs those penalties. One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which violates the resilience requirement. Deep Archive cannot provide millisecond access.

question: A media analytics company has a 5 PB data lake with unpredictable access patterns. Many objects are not touched for more than 6 months, and the applications can wait several hours when they occasionally need one of those objects. The company wants to minimize storage cost automatically without building lifecycle rules for each dataset. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Add a single lifecycle rule that transitions every object in the data lake to S3 Standard-IA 30 days after creation.
Store all objects in S3 One Zone-IA, which costs about 20% less than S3 Standard-IA.
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering and activate the optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers.
Store all objects in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, the lowest-cost class for long-lived, rarely accessed data that needs millisecond access.
explanation: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects among tiers automatically based on access, and the optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers place long-untouched objects in archive pricing when applications can tolerate asynchronous restore times. A fixed Standard-IA rule does not adapt and incurs retrieval fees for popular data. One Zone-IA reduces resilience and is not an archive price. Glacier Instant Retrieval charges higher retrieval fees for frequently accessed data and is not the cheapest for objects untouched for months.

question: Once a year, an auditing firm must restore 40 TB of records stored in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class. The restore can take up to 12 hours. Which retrieval option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Expedited retrieval
Standard retrieval
Copy the objects to S3 Standard with S3 Batch Operations without restoring them
Bulk retrieval
explanation: Bulk retrievals are the lowest-cost option for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and typically finish within 5 to 12 hours, which fits the window. Expedited and Standard retrievals are faster but cost more. Objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval must be restored before they can be copied, so a copy without a restore fails.

question: A bank must keep a continuously updated copy of production data from one account in a test account. Data residency rules require that the data never leave the eu-central-1 Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure S3 Same-Region Replication from the production bucket to a test account bucket in eu-central-1.
Configure Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in the test account in eu-west-1, which is also an EU Region.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and have the test account download new objects as they arrive.
Schedule a Lambda function that copies new objects to the test account bucket in eu-central-1 every night.
explanation: Same-Region Replication automatically and asynchronously copies new objects to a bucket in another account within the same Region, keeping the data in eu-central-1. Cross-Region Replication moves data to another Region and breaks residency rules. Transfer Acceleration is not a replication mechanism. A nightly copy job adds code to maintain and is not continuous.

question: A company replicates a critical bucket to a backup bucket in another Region. It is concerned that a compromised user could delete data in the source bucket and that the deletions would propagate to the backup. Which replication behavior protects the backup copy?
options: Enable delete marker replication on the replication rule so that the backup always mirrors the exact state of the source.
Leave delete marker replication off; S3 never replicates versioned deletes, so prior versions stay in the destination.
Enable S3 Replication Time Control so that 99.99% of objects replicate within 15 minutes of being uploaded.
Change the rule from Cross-Region Replication to Same-Region Replication and enable replica modification sync.
explanation: When a delete request specifies a version ID, S3 does not replicate the permanent deletion, and simple deletes that create delete markers are replicated only if delete marker replication is turned on. Enabling delete marker replication would make objects appear deleted in the backup. RTC only speeds up replication, including of delete markers when enabled. Switching to SRR does not change delete behavior.

question: A team wants to stop creating new object versions in a bucket that has had versioning enabled for a year. What happens when the team changes the bucket's versioning configuration?
options: Versioning can be suspended, and existing object versions remain in the bucket until they are deleted.
Versioning can be disabled, and all noncurrent versions are deleted immediately.
Versioning can be disabled, and all existing versions are merged into a single null version.
The versioning configuration cannot be changed once enabled, so the bucket must be deleted.
explanation: Once versioning is enabled, a bucket can only be returned to a suspended state, never to unversioned. Suspending stops new versions from being created, but all existing versions stay and continue to be billed until they are deleted manually or by lifecycle rules. Versions are not deleted or merged automatically, and the bucket does not need to be recreated.

question: A solutions architect configures an S3 event notification that targets a standard SQS queue, but saving the configuration fails with an error that S3 cannot validate the destination. What should the architect do?
options: Enable versioning on the source bucket and then save the event notification configuration again.
Attach an IAM role to the bucket that trusts s3.amazonaws.com and allows sqs:SendMessage on the queue ARN.
Add an SQS queue policy allowing the s3.amazonaws.com principal to call sqs:SendMessage, conditioned on the bucket ARN.
Convert the queue to an SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication enabled for the S3 events.
explanation: S3 publishes notifications using the S3 service principal, so the queue's resource policy must allow s3.amazonaws.com to send messages, ideally limited with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount. Versioning is not required for notifications. Buckets do not assume IAM roles for event delivery. S3 event notifications do not support FIFO queues as direct destinations.

question: An S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function that indexes each new document. During traffic spikes, the function is throttled and some documents are never indexed. The company needs every upload to be processed eventually and wants failed messages kept for investigation. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Increase the Lambda function timeout to the 15-minute maximum so that throttled invocations have time to complete.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket to smooth out bursts of incoming uploads during traffic spikes.
Send the S3 events to an SQS queue, have the Lambda function poll the queue, and attach a dead-letter queue.
Replace the event notification with an hourly EventBridge scheduled rule that lists the bucket and invokes the function.
explanation: An SQS queue durably buffers events during spikes, the Lambda event source mapping processes them as capacity allows, and a dead-letter queue keeps messages that repeatedly fail. A longer timeout does not address throttling. Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads rather than throttling them. Hourly listing adds delay and cost and still needs custom tracking of processed objects.

question: A company is worried that an attacker with administrator access to its production account could delete or encrypt all S3 backups. The company needs an immutable copy of new backup objects that administrators of the production account cannot delete for 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Enable versioning and MFA Delete on the production backup bucket so that permanent deletes require the root user's MFA code.
Replicate the backups to a bucket in a separate AWS account that has Object Lock enabled with a 30-day default retention in compliance mode.
Replicate the backups to a second versioned bucket in the production account with delete marker replication enabled.
Create daily S3 Inventory reports of the backup bucket and deliver them to a bucket owned by a separate security account.
explanation: Replicating to an Object Lock bucket in a separate account isolates the copy from production administrators, and compliance mode retention prevents anyone from deleting the replicated versions for 30 days. MFA Delete in the same account can still be used by a privileged attacker with the root MFA device and offers no account isolation. A second bucket in the same account with delete marker replication propagates deletes. Inventory reports list objects but do not back them up.
subtopic: Ransomware protection with replication and Object Lock

question: A public sector agency serves a static website from an S3 bucket in us-east-1 through CloudFront. The site must remain available even if S3 in us-east-1 becomes unavailable, with no manual intervention. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Configure Same-Region Replication from the primary bucket to a second bucket in us-east-1 owned by another account.
Configure Cross-Region Replication from the primary bucket to a bucket in us-west-2.
Store the site objects in S3 One Zone-IA so that only one Availability Zone must be available to serve them.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the primary bucket so that CloudFront can reach it through other edge locations.
Create a CloudFront origin group with the primary bucket and the us-west-2 bucket, failing over on 5xx responses.
explanation: Cross-Region Replication keeps a copy of the site in another Region, and a CloudFront origin group automatically retries GET requests against the secondary origin when the primary returns errors. A second bucket in the same Region does not protect against a Regional S3 problem. One Zone-IA reduces resilience. Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads and does not provide failover.

question: EC2 instances in private subnets must read and write objects in an S3 bucket in the same Region. Traffic must not traverse the internet, and the bucket must reject any request that does not come through the company's VPC endpoint. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Route S3 traffic through a NAT gateway and allow only the NAT gateway's Elastic IP address in the bucket policy.
Create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and require the aws:SecureTransport condition.
Move the instances to public subnets and assign public IP addresses.
Add a bucket policy that denies all requests unless aws:SourceVpce equals the VPC endpoint ID.
explanation: A gateway endpoint adds route table entries so S3 traffic stays on the AWS network without a NAT gateway, and a bucket policy that denies requests not made through that endpoint enforces the restriction. A NAT gateway sends traffic to the public S3 endpoint and adds data processing charges. Transfer Acceleration uses edge locations over the internet. Public subnets expose the instances unnecessarily.

question: A high-traffic analytics platform reads and writes thousands of SSE-KMS encrypted objects per second in one bucket by using a customer managed key. The applications intermittently receive KMS ThrottlingException errors, causing failed S3 requests. The company must keep using the customer managed key. Which solution will resolve the issue with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Replace the key with a multi-Region key and spread the S3 requests across the Regions that hold replica keys.
Enable S3 Bucket Keys for the bucket so that S3 makes far fewer requests to AWS KMS.
Distribute the objects across more prefixes in the bucket so that each prefix gets its own request rate limit.
Switch the bucket's encryption to SSE-C so that S3 no longer makes any requests to AWS KMS.
explanation: With SSE-KMS, each object operation normally calls KMS and counts against the account's KMS request quota; S3 Bucket Keys let S3 generate data keys from a bucket-level key, which sharply reduces KMS calls and throttling. Multi-Region keys do not reduce per-Region request volume for this workload. More prefixes raise S3 request limits, not KMS limits. SSE-C would drop the required customer managed KMS key.

question: A mobile game downloads a single configuration object from S3 when it starts. After a viral launch, the game receives more than 20,000 GET requests per second for that one object, and many requests fail with HTTP 503 Slow Down responses. Which solution will MOST effectively resolve the issue?
options: Serve the object through Amazon CloudFront so that edge locations cache it and absorb most of the requests.
Spread the object across multiple prefixes by renaming it, because S3 scales request rates per prefix.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket so that players connect to it through the nearest CloudFront edge location.
Move the object to S3 Standard-IA under a new key name in a separate prefix of the bucket.
explanation: CloudFront caches the object at edge locations, so most requests never reach S3, removing the per-prefix request pressure and lowering latency for players. A single object lives under a single key, so adding prefixes does not split requests for that object. Transfer Acceleration still sends every request to the bucket. Standard-IA adds retrieval charges and does not raise request limits.

question: Engineering offices in Singapore and Tokyo upload 5 GB CAD archives to an S3 bucket in eu-west-1 over the internet. Uploads are slow and a single network error forces the whole file to be sent again. Which combination of actions will MOST improve upload performance and reliability? (Select TWO.)
options: Upload directly to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class by setting the storage class header on each PUT.
Enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode on the bucket to protect each uploaded archive.
Use multipart upload and send the parts in parallel so that failed parts can be retried individually.
Enable S3 server access logging to diagnose slow requests and retry failed uploads based on the logs.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and upload through the accelerate endpoint.
explanation: Multipart upload sends parts in parallel for higher throughput and only failed parts need to be resent, and Transfer Acceleration routes the traffic through nearby edge locations and the AWS backbone to the distant Region. Choosing Deep Archive changes the storage price, not upload speed. Object Lock and access logging do not improve upload performance.

question: A document management application runs on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Users upload files of up to 2 GB through the application servers, which then write them to S3. During business hours the instances are saturated by upload traffic. Which solution will MOST improve the scalability of the application?
options: Increase the ALB idle timeout so that long uploads do not fail.
Add an EBS volume to each instance to buffer uploads before copying them to S3.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration while keeping uploads flowing through the instances.
Have the application return presigned URLs so that browsers upload files directly to S3.
explanation: Presigned URLs let clients upload directly to S3, which scales automatically, while the application only authorizes the upload, removing the data path from the instances. A longer timeout and EBS buffering keep the instances in the data path. Transfer Acceleration would only speed the instance-to-S3 leg while the instances remain the bottleneck.

question: A company hosts a single-page application in an S3 bucket that has static website hosting enabled. An Amazon CloudFront distribution uses the bucket's website endpoint as a custom origin. A new security policy requires the bucket to block all public access and to accept requests only from the CloudFront distribution. Which change will meet these requirements?
options: Keep the website endpoint as the custom origin, attach an origin access control to it, and allow only the distribution's ARN in the bucket policy.
Keep the website endpoint as the origin and add a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject only from the CloudFront origin-facing IP address ranges.
Switch the origin to the bucket's REST API endpoint with an origin access control, set a default root object, and allow only the distribution in the bucket policy.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration, use the accelerate endpoint as the CloudFront origin, and turn on S3 Block Public Access for the bucket.
explanation: An S3 website endpoint supports only publicly readable content and does not support HTTPS, so it cannot serve a bucket that blocks all public access, and OAC is designed for the REST API endpoint. The REST API endpoint supports private content, so CloudFront can sign requests with OAC while the bucket policy allows only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal for that distribution, and a default root object replaces the website index document at the root. An IP-based policy still requires the website content to be public, and Transfer Acceleration is an upload optimization, not an access control.
